facts.title: The last lanthanide standing
facts.text: Lutetium has atomic number 71, making it the final member of the lanthanide series and the densest and hardest of them all. With its 4f electron shell completely filled (configuration [Xe]4f¹⁴5d¹6s²), it behaves more like a transition metal than its softer rare-earth cousins. This full f-shell also makes it unusually stable and resistant to chemical surprises.

facts.title: Discovered by three at once
facts.text: In 1907 lutetium was independently identified by Georges Urbain in Paris, Carl Auer von Welsbach in Austria, and Charles James in the United States, all within months of each other. They had each pulled it out of the mineral ytterbia, which turned out to be a mixture of two elements rather than one. A bitter priority dispute followed, but Urbain's claim ultimately won official recognition.

facts.title: Named after ancient Paris
facts.text: The name comes from Lutetia, the Latin name for Paris, the city where Georges Urbain did his work. For years some chemists, especially in Germany, instead called it cassiopeium after the constellation, a name pushed by von Welsbach. The international community eventually settled on lutetium, but the symbol was shortened from the original Lu spelling debates only in the mid-20th century.

facts.title: Stubbornly hard to separate
facts.text: Lutetium is one of the most difficult rare earths to isolate because it clings tightly to its chemical neighbors, especially ytterbium. Early chemists needed thousands of tedious fractional crystallizations to get even tiny amounts of pure salt. Pure lutetium metal was not produced in any meaningful quantity until the 1950s, decades after its discovery.

facts.title: A built-in atomic clock
facts.text: Natural lutetium contains about 2.6% of the radioactive isotope lutetium-176, which decays into hafnium-176 with a half-life of roughly 37 billion years. Geologists use this lutetium-hafnium decay as a dating tool to measure the ages of meteorites and the oldest rocks on Earth. Because the half-life is far longer than the age of the universe, only a small fraction has ever decayed.

facts.title: Rarer and pricier than gold
facts.text: Despite its name suggesting abundance, lutetium is the least abundant of the naturally occurring rare-earth elements in Earth's crust. Its scarcity and the expense of separating it make it one of the most costly rare earths, historically running into hundreds of dollars per gram for the pure metal. It is mined mainly as a byproduct from monazite ores in China, Australia, and the United States.

facts.title: Fighting cancer from the inside
facts.text: Lutetium-177 has become a star in nuclear medicine, used in targeted radiotherapy for neuroendocrine tumors and metastatic prostate cancer. Attached to molecules that home in on cancer cells, it delivers short-range beta radiation that destroys tumors while sparing nearby healthy tissue. Drugs such as Lutathera and Pluvicto, both approved in recent years, rely on this isotope.

facts.title: The fastest scintillator
facts.text: Crystals of lutetium oxyorthosilicate, known as LSO, glow brightly and extremely quickly when struck by gamma rays, making them ideal detectors. They are widely used in PET scanners, where speed and brightness translate into sharper medical images. This application consumes a notable share of the world's lutetium supply.

facts.title: A catalyst in your gas tank's cousin
facts.text: Lutetium is used in small amounts as a catalyst in petroleum cracking, the refining process that breaks heavy crude oil into gasoline and other fuels. It also serves in alkylation, hydrogenation, and polymerization reactions in the chemical industry. Its full f-shell gives it a predictable, single +3 oxidation state that chemists find easy to work with.

facts.title: No job in living things
facts.text: Lutetium has no known biological role in any organism and is not required for life. It has low toxicity, partly because its compounds dissolve poorly and the body absorbs very little of it. Animal studies suggest it is only mildly hazardous, though like all rare earths it is handled with care in laboratories and industry.
